title: The Recruiting Mistake That Stalls Founders Scaling Up (October 2026)
summary: Avoid the most common recruiting mistake founders make when scaling hiring, based on lessons from 100+ startups in 2026.
body_markdown:
One of the[recruiting mistakes that stall founders scaling up](https://www.dover.com/) is judging candidate sources by just two numbers: cost-per-hire and time-to-hire. Those metrics skip over how each source’s funnel actually behaves. Missing that shape leads to a recruiting mix that looks fine on paper and still stalls out.


**TLDR:**


-


Comparing candidate sources only on cost-per-hire or time-to-hire misses how each source’s funnel shape differs.


-


LinkedIn job postings generate high application volume but typically yield a 1-3% qualified interview rate.


-


Outbound recruiting reaches the broadest candidate pool but demands the most time to produce results.


-


Referrals and outbound produce the highest candidate quality, but each hits depth limits at scale.


-


Track cost, workload, depth, latency, and funnel conversion across every channel to build a mix that holds.


## What Is a Candidate Source?


A candidate source is any pool of candidates that you can get into your interview process.


Some examples of candidate sources:


-


LinkedIn


-


job applicants from a job posting on Indeed


-


an employee’s network


-


Wellfound


-


candidates introduced to you by a contingency recruiter


-


…and so on


Candidate sources generally fall into one of three channels:


-


referrals (network-based)


-


inbound (candidates find you)


-


outbound (you find the candidates)


When making the first one or two hires at your company, founders should focus on a single candidate source: the founders’ personal network. Early on, the main thing your company has is the founding team itself, and[your network holds your most trusted candidates.](https://www.dover.com/blog/3-keys-to-recruiting-from-your-network-without-feeling-awkward-about-it)


Once you start to scale and have some more resources to devote to hiring, you will need to start expanding to more candidate sources.


The candidate pool from each candidate source will be slightly different. Some candidate sources contain primarily active candidates (job applicants) while some are mostly passive (LinkedIn). Some are prequalified with a phone screen (contingency recruiters) while others are not.


Founders often make an apples-to-apples comparison between candidate sources without taking into account the inherent differences between them and how those will affect their hiring outcomes. Ignoring the differences between candidate sources leads to problems across your entire recruiting process, such as increasing your time to hire, wasting your team’s time, and missing out on the best candidates.


## Every Candidate Source Has Tradeoffs


Below are a few common mistakes I’ve seen dozens of companies make when weighing which candidate sources to invest in.


### Candidate Source: LinkedIn Job Posting


Summary: A job posted to LinkedIn will have a lot of applicants, but very few will be qualified for a phone screen.


Posting a job to LinkedIn will give you a rush of dopamine (by design), as you’ll usually see dozens of applications within hours of posting. But most candidates applying on LinkedIn are poor fits, in our experience working with early-stage companies: most see roughly a 1-3% interview rate from this applicant pool. LinkedIn advertises your job in front of the most active candidates first, so there is a steep drop-off in applicants after the first few days of posting.


### Candidate Source: Wellfound Outreach


Summary: Reaching out to candidates on Wellfound (formerly AngelList, which rebranded its talent product to Wellfound in 2022) leads to high response rates to your messages, but low candidate depth.


Wellfound attracts candidates who specifically want to work at a startup, even one that isn’t well-known yet. After a few hours of outbound on the platform, you’ll likely get a solid number of first phone calls scheduled.


But as you’re scaling up hiring, you’ll quickly go through the top candidates on the platform. You’ll have to reach out to either less active candidates or less qualified candidates, increasing the number of hours you’ll need to put in to make a hire.


### Candidate Source: Pre-Vetted Platforms


Summary: Pre-vetted or assessed candidate platforms often have high candidate quality, but low offer-to-hire conversion.


Pre-vetted platforms vet engineering candidates with a thorough technical process before admitting them to their marketplace, giving companies a pool of people more likely to pass a technical bar and onsite. Candidates who clear an assessment ahead of time tend to pass your onsite at a higher rate than candidates sourced elsewhere.


The catch is that these platforms often appeal to candidates running a competitive interview process with many companies at once. Since candidates get a fast-track to onsites, they tend to rack up more interviews and more offers, which lowers the offer-to-hire conversion for any single company on the platform. Larger, better-known companies tend to win these candidates on compensation, so smaller startups without a lot of name recognition may find it harder to compete, and your team can end up spending a lot of time on onsites for candidates who don’t end up closing.


### Candidate Source: LinkedIn Outreach


Summary: Sending outbound emails to passive candidates will yield the highest candidate quality and depth, but requires a large time commitment to execute.


[Outbound recruiting](https://blog.dover.io/its-time-outbound-worked/) gives you the[largest possible candidate pool](https://scionstaffing.com/recruiting-passive-candidates-strategic-approach/) : everyone. If your startup can get people excited in just a few sentences, then outbound may be a good fit for you. Typically, outbound is the most time-consuming of the three recruiting channels, so you’ll have to dedicate a lot more time to it (unless you’re using Dover).


The downside with outbound is that sometimes candidates are open to chatting on the phone just to network with you, and aren’t actually ready to switch jobs.[Passive candidates](https://www.icims.com/blog/passive-candidate-sourcing-made-simple/) may also have less urgency throughout the interview process, slowing down the time-to-hire.


### Candidate Source: Employee Referrals


Summary: Employee referrals will have[high candidate quality and response rates](https://erinapp.com/blog/employee-referral-statistics-you-need-to-know-for-2025-a-game-changer-for-enterprise-recruitment/) but very limited depth.


Your employees know your company and your culture best. They can make the best recommendations on who in their network could be a good fit for your company. But these candidates often aren’t actively looking, and there are some diversity risks through scaling up a recruiting strategy entirely through referrals.


## How the Hiring Market Has Shifted in 2026


The core tradeoffs between candidate sources haven’t changed, but the conditions have. Startup hiring volume is lower than the 2021-2022 peak. AI-assisted outbound sourcing has lowered the per-hour cost of reaching passive candidates, but it has also raised the noise floor, so message quality and company reputation matter more as filters. Startups that bring recruiters in earlier tend to move faster through the funnel, a sign that the coordination layer, as much as the sourcing channel, is where impact is often won or lost.


## Cover All Your Bases


As you can start to see, each candidate source has many tradeoffs that need to be considered when building up a well-rounded recruiting strategy. You must weigh each candidate source on a few different dimensions to make sure you’re using the combination that’s right given your stage of company, your desired workload, and your candidate bar.


Here are the most important variables to keep an eye on for each recruiting channel:


Candidate Source Volume Candidate Quality Depth at Scale Time Commitment Key Tradeoff


LinkedIn Job Posting High Low (1-3% interview rate) Limited (drops off after a few days) Low High volume, low signal-to-noise ratio


Wellfound Outreach Moderate Moderate Low (pool thins quickly) Moderate High response rates, but limited depth


Pre-Vetted Platforms Low-Moderate High (pre-vetted candidates) Moderate Moderate High quality, but low offer-to-hire conversion


LinkedIn Outreach (Outbound) Very High (broadest pool) High High High Best quality and depth, most time-intensive


Employee Referrals Low High Very Low (network finite) Low High quality and response rates, limited depth


-


Cost: how much do you spend per applicant, phone screen, and hire?


-


Workload: how much time is spent per week to get a candidate to convert (i.e. get to a phone screen)? Also, who is doing the work (a founder, a hiring manager, or recruiter)?


-


Depth: how many good first phone screens per week you can get?


-


Latency: how long does it take you to make the hire?


-


[Funnel conversion](https://www.dover.com/blog/recruiting-metrics-startup-hiring) : what percentage of candidates make it past the each stage in the process (phone screen, technical assessment, onsite, offer)? How does your funnel compare to benchmarks?


These role-specific variables will also have an effect on which channels you should finally decide to use:


-


Role type: hiring an engineer (hard market) will take longer than hiring an account executive (softer market)


-


Geography: hiring remotely will give you more depth instead of restricting candidates to one city


-


Channel source type:[inbound channels](https://www.dover.com/blog/our-take-on-a-successful-inbound-recruiting-strategy) will deliver a higher volume of candidates, but a lower signal-to-noise ratio


Taking a[multi-channel recruiting approach](https://www.dover.com/blog/sources-of-recruitment) and drawing on all candidate sources will make your recruiting faster, more effective, and more affordable.


Dover’s model is one concrete version of this framework: a free ATS paired with a marketplace of fractional recruiters, with per-hire cost typically averaging $4.8k depending on the role and search. A hiring manager and a fractional recruiter working the same search see candidate status and sourcing activity for every channel in one shared pipeline.


## How Dover Fits Into This Framework


A free applicant tracking system can serve as the shared layer that keeps multi-channel sourcing coherent. Instead of inbound applications, outbound outreach, and referral introductions living in separate tools or spreadsheets, a single pipeline holds candidate status, source, and funnel stage for every channel at once. This matters most once a team moves past the founder’s personal network and starts running LinkedIn postings, outbound sequences, and referral requests at the same time, since that’s when duplicate outreach and missed handoffs tend to show up.


On top of that shared pipeline, Dover pairs the free ATS with a recruiter marketplace:[fractional recruiters](https://www.dover.com/blog/what-is-a-fractional-recruiter-guide) set their own pricing (hourly, retainer, or pay-per-hire), with Dover’s average cost per hire at $4.8k and no long-term contract required. A company can bring in a recruiter for a single hard-to-fill role without a long-term commitment, then scale that support up or down as hiring needs change.


The structural advantage of this shared-system model is visibility. Because recruiters and internal teams work from the same pipeline instead of parallel spreadsheets, both sides can see sourcing activity and funnel conversion across every channel in real time, which makes it easier to spot where a candidate source is underperforming before it quietly drains the team’s workload.


## FAQs


### What is the difference between inbound, outbound, and referral candidate sources?


Inbound candidates find you through job postings. Outbound means you reach out to passive candidates. Referrals are introductions from employees or the founding team. Each has a distinct funnel shape: inbound brings high volume with low signal-to-noise, outbound offers the broadest pool but takes the most time, and referrals bring strong quality with limited depth.


### Why shouldn’t I weigh candidate sources purely on cost-per-hire or time-to-hire?


Those two metrics capture only part of the picture. A LinkedIn posting may look cheap per application, but if only 1-3% of applicants are qualified, screening time climbs quickly. A platform like Triplebyte can cut time to onsite yet lower offer-to-hire conversion, since candidates interview at many companies at once. Tracking funnel conversion at each stage shows where time and money actually go.


### Which candidate source delivers the highest-quality candidates?


Employee referrals and outbound recruiting (e.g., LinkedIn outreach to passive candidates) consistently produce the highest quality. Referrals carry built-in trust, since employees can assess fit firsthand. Outbound reaches people not actively job-hunting. The tradeoff is limited depth for referrals and a heavy time cost for outbound, so neither holds up alone at scale.


## Final Thoughts on Candidate Sources


The[recruiting mistakes that stall founders scaling up](https://www.dover.com/) often come down to one blind spot: not understanding the funnel shape each channel produces. Building across multiple candidate sources is not about picking a winner. It is about assembling a mix that fits where your company is today. Inbound keeps the top of the funnel full. Outbound reaches people who will never apply. Referrals shortcut trust. The challenge is running all three without losing visibility. Dover’s model handles that directly: a free ATS that serves as the infrastructure layer for multi-channel hiring, with a marketplace of fractional recruiters, each with vetted client reviews, available when a search needs more hands-on work, typically averaging $4.8k per hire with no long-term contracts required.
